citation: Mayer, R. E., Makransky, G., & Parong, J. (2023). The promise and pitfalls of learning in immersive virtual reality. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction, 39(11), 2229–2238. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2022.2108563 (Published online 18 Aug 2022; print issue dated 2023 per journal citation header — manifest lists 2022.)
discipline: educational psychology / instructional design (cognitive theory of multimedia learning)
thesis: A narrative self-review of the authors' own IVR-learning research program, organized around media-comparison experiments (IVR vs. slideshow/desktop/video controls) and value-added experiments (adding design or generative-learning features to IVR itself). Argues immersion's promise is motivation-driven generative processing and its pitfall is distraction-driven extraneous processing; concludes that methods/value-added design, not the media itself, should guide IVR instructional practice, since 20 years of media-comparison work shows no reliable IVR advantage while value-added work reliably improves IVR's own effectiveness (pp. 2229-2230, 2235-2236).

sections.title: 1. Objective and rationale for learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Frames IVR as 'active media' (physically engaged learner) against passive slideshow media, using a human-bloodstream lesson example; states the paper reviews the authors' own media-comparison and value-added research rather than the broader literature (pp. 2229-2230).

sections.title: 2. Introduction to learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Defines immersion as an objective property of delivery technology and presence as the learner's subjective feeling of 'being there' (citing Witmer & Singer 1998); sets out three immersion levels — no immersion (narrated slideshow), low immersion (2D desktop VR), high immersion (HMD-delivered 3D), the last of which the paper calls IVR (p. 2230).

sections.title: 3. Theoretical foundations of learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Grounds the review in Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning: limited cognitive capacity is divided among extraneous, essential, and generative processing. A promise/pitfall table frames IVR's 'promise' (immersion -> motivation -> generative processing) against its 'pitfall' (immersion -> arousal/perceptual richness -> extraneous processing, at the cost of essential processing) (pp. 2230-2231).

sections.title: 4. Media comparison research on learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Summarizes 13 IVR-vs-conventional-media experiments (Design-a-Plant, The Body VR bloodstream lesson, Kokoda WWII history, Labster science-lab sim) using Cohen's d on transfer-test scores; overall pattern is a negligible-to-negative median effect for IVR, with IVR learners showing more self-reported distraction and higher biometric (heart-rate/EEG) arousal (pp. 2231-2232).

sections.title: 5. Value-added research on learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Summarizes studies comparing IVR-with-added-feature to plain IVR: instructional-design principles (modality, personalization, pre-training) and generative-learning-activity principles (summarizing, question-answering, enacting), plus gender-matching of the onscreen agent and home-vs-school deployment. Most added features raise transfer scores; gender-matching and home-venue delivery show weaker/negligible effects (pp. 2232-2235).

sections.title: 6. Future directions for research on learning in immersive virtual reality
sections.summary: Draws two conclusions: no strong evidence IVR beats conventional media for academic content, but instructional-design and generative-activity additions can improve IVR's effectiveness. Proposes further research on exposure/familiarity effects, on which content domains (e.g., procedural/dangerous skills like surgery) best suit IVR, and on usability/motion-sickness constraints (pp. 2235-2236).

sections.title: 7. Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates the promise/pitfall framing and the methods-not-media, value-added conclusion: the open challenge is reducing IVR's distracting (extraneous-processing) aspects while preserving its motivating (generative-processing) aspects and managing essential processing (p. 2236).

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: defined per Witmer & Singer (1998, p.225) as the learner's subjective feeling of being in an artificially created place; distinguished from immersion as subjective/learner-focused vs. objective/technology-focused (Table 1)

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: objective property of delivery technology, gauged by display/rendering quality; operationalized as a three-level scale (no/low/high immersion) structuring every experiment in the paper

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: the paper's own CTML vocabulary — extraneous / essential / generative processing — normalized to this axis: extraneous processing ~ extraneous load, generative processing ~ germane processing, essential processing ~ intrinsic/essential load in the material (source's own terms recorded; mapping is P/anticipatory-application)

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: the 'promise' route: high immersion is claimed to raise motivation, channeling into generative processing; tested once directly — enjoyment ratings for IVR-with-summarizing did not differ from IVR-without-summarizing

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: sole outcome measure across both research programs: post-lesson transfer-test scores reported as Cohen's d

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.treatment: high-immersion condition in all 13 media-comparison and 12 value-added studies; associated with elevated self-reported distraction and biometric (heart-rate/EEG) arousal in the two studies reporting those measures

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.treatment: low-immersion control/comparator: Design-a-Plant and Labster desktop deliveries

conditions.label: 2D video / slideshow / text
conditions.treatment: no-immersion control: narrated slideshow (Body VR comparison) and interactive desktop video (Kokoda comparison)

conditions.label: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.treatment: general framing applied across Table 5's control arms, contrasted with IVR's 'active media' framing

conditions.label: home vs classroom setting
conditions.treatment: one value-added study (Table 6 line 12, feeds ped-sec-12) compares IVR delivery at home vs. in school; finds equivalence

readings.claim: IVR's instructional promise (motivation -> generative processing) and its pitfall (distraction/arousal -> extraneous processing) are two faces of the same immersion mechanism.
Across 13 media-comparison experiments spanning four lesson families, the median transfer-test effect size for IVR vs. conventional media is negligible-to-negative.

IVR learners report higher distraction and show higher biometric (heart-rate/EEG) arousal than learners using conventional media, drawn specifically from the Parong & Mayer studies built here as ped-sec-13.
There is not yet strong evidence that students learn academic material more deeply in IVR than with conventional media.

Instructional-design principles (modality, personalization, pre-training) and generative-activity principles (summarizing, answering, enacting) can improve IVR's own instructional effectiveness, largely independent of media-comparison outcomes.
Gender-matching the onscreen pedagogical agent and moving delivery from school to home show weak or negligible learning effects; the home-venue finding is framed as a positive equivalence result.
The open instructional-design challenge is managing the promise/pitfall trade-off within IVR itself, not choosing IVR over conventional media or the reverse.

tensions.axis: media-comparison findings (null/negative) vs. value-added findings (largely positive)
tensions.note: The paper's own two research programs point in different directions: comparing IVR to other media yields no reliable advantage, while adding design/generative features to IVR itself reliably helps — the tension the 'methods-not-media' conclusion is built to resolve.

The paper frames both as live, co-occurring effects of the same immersion mechanism rather than resolving in favor of one; Phase 3 synthesis should not flatten this dual-path framing into a single-cause account.

tensions.axis: behavioral activity vs. cognitive activity ('active learning')
tensions.note: The paper explicitly warns against assuming physically active media (IVR) produces cognitively active learning, or that passive media produces passive learning; citing Kirschner et al. and Chi & Wylie's ICAP framework.
